title: Build and query with Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.q: Your AI API makes many short-lived database calls and you enable the built-in PgBouncer. Which port should the app connect to?

options.why: 443 is HTTPS, not a PostgreSQL port.
Correct. PgBouncer connections use port 6432.
5432 is the standard direct PostgreSQL port.
1433 is the SQL Server port.

questions.hint: PgBouncer listens on a different port from PostgreSQL itself.
questions.explain: Enable PgBouncer in server configuration and connect on 6432.

questions.q: Which PostgreSQL extension provides trigram-based fuzzy text matching for autocomplete?

options.why: Correct. pg_trgm provides trigram text similarity.
hstore adds a key-value data type.
pgvector adds vector types and similarity search.
PostGIS is for geospatial capabilities.

questions.hint: Fuzzy matching splits text into groups of three characters.
questions.explain: pgvector for embeddings, pg_trgm for fuzzy text, hstore for key-value pairs.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A team runs a Burstable-tier Azure Database for PostgreSQL server for a proof of concept.

rows.text: They can enable the built-in PgBouncer on this tier.
rows.why: PgBouncer isn't available on the Burstable tier.

rows.text: They can move to General Purpose later with a brief restart.
rows.why: Compute tiers can be changed after deployment with a brief restart.

rows.text: Backups are kept for 35 days unless they change it.
rows.why: Default retention is seven days; you can extend it up to 35.

rows.text: A point-in-time restore creates a new server instance.
rows.why: Restore creates a new server at the chosen timestamp.

questions.hint: Burstable is for dev and doesn't get every feature. Backups default to a week, and a restore makes a new server.
questions.explain: Know the tier limits, backup defaults and how restores work.

questions.q: An AI service keeps large working sets in memory and runs complex analytical queries alongside vector operations. Which compute tier fits best?

options.why: General Purpose is balanced, not memory-heavy.
Correct. High memory-to-vCPU ratios suit large in-memory sets and analytical queries.
Burstable suits dev and intermittent workloads.

options.text: Any tier, because storage scales separately
options.why: Storage scaling doesn't provide the memory this workload needs.

questions.hint: Large in-memory working sets point to the tier named after memory.
questions.explain: Memory Optimized for in-memory and analytical work; General Purpose for steady production.

questions.q: Yesterday a script dropped the conversations table on a production server. Backups use the default settings. How do you recover the data?

options.text: Point-in-time restore, which rolls the existing server back in place
options.why: A restore creates a new server instance. It doesn't overwrite the existing one.

options.text: You can't: backups are kept for 24 hours
options.why: The default retention is seven days.

options.text: Point-in-time restore into a new server
options.why: Correct. PITR recovers to any moment within retention (seven days by default) into a new server.

options.text: Open a support ticket, because backups must be requested in advance
options.why: Backups are automatic, so you can restore yourself.

questions.hint: Automatic backups allow recovery to a point in time. Where does the restored data end up?
questions.explain: Backups are automatic, with seven days' retention by default (configurable up to 35). Point-in-time restore recovers to any moment in that window and creates a new server instance.

questions.q: Two applications share one Azure Database for PostgreSQL server. They must never see each other's data, and each needs its own backup and restore. How should you organize them?

options.text: Put both applications in one database, with a table prefix per app
options.why: Prefixes don't isolate data or give independent restores.

options.text: Use one database and give each application its own schema
options.why: Schemas organize objects inside a database. Learn suggests separate databases for full isolation and independent restore.

options.text: Create one table per application inside the postgres system database
options.why: The system database isn't meant for application data, and this doesn't isolate anything.

options.text: Give each application its own database on the server
options.why: Correct. Separate databases give complete isolation and independent backup and restore.

questions.hint: A server can host several databases. When does Learn say to separate them?
questions.explain: A server can host multiple databases, each isolated. Use separate databases for complete isolation between applications or independent backup and restore.

questions.q: Production code must make sure it's talking to the genuine Azure PostgreSQL server, checking both the certificate authority and the hostname. Which sslmode should it use?

options.why: require encrypts but doesn't validate certificates.
prefer doesn't validate certificates.
Correct. verify-full validates the CA and confirms the hostname.
verify-ca validates the CA but not the hostname.

questions.hint: There's an sslmode that checks both the certificate chain and the host name.
questions.explain: Use verify-full in production.

questions.q: An Azure-hosted app uses a managed identity to connect with Microsoft Entra authentication. Which resource should it request a token for?

options.why: That's Key Vault.
Correct. Entra identities obtain tokens from this resource and use them as the password.
That's the Azure Resource Manager audience.
That isn't the PostgreSQL token resource Learn names.

questions.hint: Entra tokens for Azure's open-source databases come from one specific resource URL.
questions.explain: credential.get_token("https://ossrdbms-aad.database.windows.net/.default")

questions.q: Put the Microsoft Entra connection flow in order.
steps: The application requests an access token from Microsoft Entra ID
Entra validates the identity and returns a token
The application connects to PostgreSQL using the token as the password
PostgreSQL validates the token against the configured Entra administrator
questions.hint: Get a token, Entra issues it, connect with it as the password, and the server checks it.
questions.explain: Tokens are short-lived, so no password is stored.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A developer can't connect from a laptop to a server that uses **private access** with VNet integration.

rows.text: Adding the laptop's IP to firewall rules is the fix Learn describes for private access.
rows.why: Firewall rules apply to public access; private access is reachable only from the VNet, peered networks or VPN/ExpressRoute.

rows.text: Connecting through a VPN into the virtual network is a valid path.
rows.why: Private access works through VPN or ExpressRoute.

rows.text: A client using sslmode=disable would be rejected even on the right network.
TLS 1.0 connections are accepted for older clients.

questions.hint: Private access means connecting from inside the network. TLS is always required.
questions.explain: Know the two networking models and the TLS requirements.

questions.q: A legacy reporting tool can only connect with TLS 1.0, and its connections to Azure Database for PostgreSQL are rejected. What does the server enforce?

options.text: TLS by default, with TLS 1.2 and 1.3 supported
options.why: Correct. Older TLS versions are rejected, so the tool needs an upgrade.

options.text: Plain TCP unless a certificate is installed on the server
options.why: The managed server already requires TLS. You don't install certificates on it.

options.text: Encryption for connections from outside Azure, plain TCP inside
options.why: All connections must use TLS, wherever they come from.
The tier doesn't change the TLS versions accepted.

questions.hint: Which TLS versions does the managed service accept?
questions.explain: Azure Database for PostgreSQL encrypts all connections with TLS. It requires TLS by default, supports TLS 1.2 and 1.3, and rejects older versions.

questions.q: Security asks why the team should move the AI API from a database password to Microsoft Entra authentication with a managed identity. Which benefit does Learn give?

options.why: TLS is still required for every connection.

options.text: No stored password: tokens are short-lived, and identity is managed centrally
options.why: Correct. Entra uses OAuth 2.0 tokens instead of passwords, which removes password storage.

options.text: Queries run faster because tokens skip permission checks
options.why: Tokens authenticate the identity. Database permissions still apply.

options.text: The app no longer needs PgBouncer
options.why: Authentication and connection pooling are separate concerns.

questions.hint: Think about what the app no longer has to keep secret.
questions.explain: Microsoft Entra authentication uses short-lived OAuth 2.0 tokens instead of passwords, giving centralized identity management and removing password storage.

questions.q: Your server uses public access. A new developer can't connect from home, although the same code works for teammates in the office. What should you check first?

options.why: TLS is required, but the difference here is location, which points to the firewall.

options.text: Whether the server has VNet integration enabled
options.why: Public access servers use firewall rules, not VNet integration.

options.text: Whether PgBouncer is enabled on port 6432
options.why: Pooling doesn't explain why one location fails and another works.

options.text: Whether the developer's IP address is allowed in the firewall rules
options.why: Correct. With public access, firewall rules control which client IPs can connect.

questions.hint: The code works from one network and not from another. What controls which clients can connect?
questions.explain: With public access, the server has a public IP and firewall rules control which client IPs can connect. If your machine can't connect, check that its IP is allowed.

questions.q: A messages table will receive billions of inserts and needs a simple auto-incrementing key. Which type fits?

options.why: Strings aren't auto-incrementing keys.
SERIAL is 32-bit and can run out above about two billion rows.
BYTEA stores binary data.
Correct. BIGSERIAL is 64-bit, for tables that may exceed two billion rows.

questions.hint: Billions of rows outgrow a 32-bit counter.
questions.explain: Use BIGSERIAL for high-volume tables; UUIDs when IDs are generated outside the database.

questions.q: You delete a conversation that still has messages referencing it, and the messages FK has no ON DELETE clause. What happens?

options.why: That's CASCADE, which you must specify.
That's SET NULL.

options.text: The messages get the column's default value
options.why: That's SET DEFAULT.
Correct. RESTRICT is the default and blocks the delete when referencing rows exist.

questions.hint: Without ON DELETE, a referenced parent can't be removed.
questions.explain: RESTRICT is the default referential action.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A table has a composite index on `(conversation_id, created_at)`.

rows.why: The index serves filters on its leading column.

rows.text: The index helps WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01' with no conversation_id filter.
rows.why: It can't serve filters on trailing columns alone.

rows.text: Every extra index adds overhead to inserts, updates and deletes.
rows.why: Indexes speed reads but cost storage and write work.

questions.hint: A composite index helps filters that start with its leading column. Every index costs on writes.
questions.explain: Column order in composite indexes matters; be selective on write-heavy tables.

questions.q: You must add a category column and an index on it together, so that either both changes apply or neither does. What should you do?

options.text: Run both statements inside BEGIN … COMMIT
options.why: Correct. Most DDL in PostgreSQL is transactional, so you can ROLLBACK if a statement fails.

options.text: Use DROP TABLE … CASCADE and recreate the table
options.why: Dropping the table loses data.

options.text: Run them separately; DDL can't be rolled back in PostgreSQL
options.why: PostgreSQL DDL is mostly transactional, unlike some databases.

options.text: Add the column with ON DELETE CASCADE
options.why: ON DELETE CASCADE is a foreign key action, not a transaction.

questions.hint: Group the changes so they succeed or fail together.
questions.explain: Wrap related schema changes in a transaction.

questions.q: A tasks table has a status column that may only hold 'pending', 'completed' or 'failed'. You want the database itself to reject any other value. What should you add?

options.why: NOT NULL stops nulls, but any other text would still be accepted.
Indexes speed up queries. They don't validate values.
A default fills in a missing value. It doesn't reject other values.
Correct. A CHECK constraint validates values against a condition.

questions.hint: Which constraint validates a value against a condition?
questions.explain: Constraints enforce rules on data: NOT NULL prevents nulls, DEFAULT provides a value, and CHECK validates values against a condition such as status IN (…).

questions.q: You need the status field from a JSONB column as text, to compare with 'active'. Which expression should you use?

options.why: -> returns JSON, not text.
? checks that the key exists.
@> tests containment of a JSON value.
Correct. ->> extracts the element as text.

questions.hint: One arrow returns JSON, and the double arrow returns text.
questions.explain: -> for JSON, ->> for text, ? for key existence, @> for containment.

questions.q: This query fails with "column msg_date does not exist": `SELECT DATE(created_at) AS msg_date FROM messages WHERE msg_date > '2024-01-01'`. Why?

options.text: WHERE runs before SELECT, so the alias isn't defined yet
options.why: Correct. Repeat the expression in WHERE, or use the alias in ORDER BY.

options.text: Aliases can't contain an underscore in PostgreSQL
options.why: Underscores are fine in aliases; the problem is when WHERE runs.

options.text: The column has to be cast to TIMESTAMPTZ first
options.why: Casting doesn't create the alias for WHERE.

options.text: DATE() isn't a supported function in PostgreSQL
options.why: DATE() works; the alias is the problem.

questions.hint: Clauses don't run in the order you write them.
questions.explain: Only clauses after SELECT (ORDER BY, LIMIT/OFFSET) can use SELECT aliases.

questions.q: An API pages through millions of messages 20 at a time, and page 1,000 has become very slow with OFFSET. What should you use instead?

options.text: Keyset pagination on (created_at, id) from the last row
options.why: Correct. Keyset pagination filters from the last seen values and stays fast at any depth; id breaks ties.

options.text: A recursive CTE that walks the messages in order
options.why: Recursive CTEs are for hierarchies.

options.text: ORDER BY created_at NULLS LAST with the same OFFSET
options.why: NULL ordering doesn't fix deep pagination.

options.text: A larger OFFSET with LIMIT 200 to cut round trips
options.why: Bigger pages still scan and discard skipped rows.

questions.hint: OFFSET reads and discards every skipped row.
questions.explain: OFFSET scans and discards skipped rows; keyset pagination doesn't.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A checkpoint write uses `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (task_id, step_number) DO UPDATE SET checkpoint_data = EXCLUDED.checkpoint_data RETURNING id, (xmax = 0) AS is_new`.

rows.text: EXCLUDED refers to the values that would have been inserted.
rows.why: EXCLUDED is the pseudo-table of proposed values.

rows.text: is_new is true when the row was updated rather than inserted.
rows.why: xmax = 0 is true for newly inserted rows.

rows.text: RETURNING gives back the id in the same round trip.
Using DO NOTHING instead would update the existing checkpoint.
rows.why: DO NOTHING skips the conflicting row.

questions.hint: EXCLUDED is the row you tried to insert, and RETURNING saves a round trip.
questions.explain: Upserts make checkpoint writes idempotent; RETURNING tells you what happened.

questions.q: A dashboard must list every conversation with its message count, including conversations that have no messages yet. Which join keeps the conversations with zero messages?

options.why: An inner join drops conversations that have no matching messages.
A cross join pairs every row with every row, which isn't a count per conversation.

options.text: message_stats WHERE conversation_id IS NOT NULL
options.why: This only returns conversations that have messages.
Correct. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table, even with no match.

questions.hint: You need every row from one side, whether or not the other side matches.
questions.explain: A LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table with matching rows from the right, filling non-matches with NULL, so conversations with zero messages stay in the result.

questions.q: You need only the conversations that have more than 100 messages, using GROUP BY conversation_id and COUNT(*). Where does the condition COUNT(*) > 100 go?

options.why: ORDER BY sorts results. It doesn't filter them.
LIMIT caps how many rows come back. It doesn't test counts.

options.text: In the WHERE clause before GROUP BY
options.why: WHERE filters rows before grouping, so the count doesn't exist yet.

options.text: In a HAVING clause after GROUP BY
options.why: Correct. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

questions.hint: Rows are filtered before grouping. Groups are filtered after.
questions.explain: WHERE filters rows before GROUP BY; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Aliases from SELECT are visible only to ORDER BY and LIMIT/OFFSET.

questions.q: A search box should find messages that contain "azure" whatever the capitalization, such as "Azure" or "AZURE". Which operator does Learn suggest?

options.why: Correct. ILIKE does case-insensitive pattern matching without LOWER().
This is case-sensitive pattern matching, and it needs the whole string to match.
LIKE is case-sensitive, so "Azure" wouldn't match.
Equality needs the whole value to match exactly.

questions.hint: There's a case-insensitive version of LIKE.
questions.explain: The ILIKE operator provides case-insensitive pattern matching without functions like LOWER(), which suits user-facing search.

questions.q: A nightly job loads 2 million chat messages into PostgreSQL from Python. Which approach does Learn say is fastest?

options.text: One INSERT per row in a loop
options.why: Individual inserts maximize round trips.
executemany suits hundreds to a few thousand rows.
Correct. COPY is often 2–10 times faster for 10,000+ rows.

options.text: An INSERT … ON CONFLICT for each row
options.why: Per-row upserts are slower still.

questions.hint: Bulk loads are fastest with PostgreSQL's dedicated copy protocol.
questions.explain: Batch with executemany for moderate sizes; use COPY for large loads.

questions.q: Match each psycopg error to the handling Learn recommends.

items.why: Transient connection failures are retry candidates.
Constraint violations need code or data changes, not retries.
PostgreSQL terminates one transaction; roll back and retry.

questions.hint: Transient errors are worth retrying. Data errors aren't.
questions.explain: Retry transient failures and deadlocks; don't retry constraint or syntax errors.

questions.q: A FastAPI service opens a new PostgreSQL connection per request and builds queries with f-strings. Which two changes follow Learn's guidance? (Select two.)

options.text: Borrow connections from a psycopg_pool ConnectionPool
options.why: Correct. Pools avoid the cost of creating connections for every request.

options.text: Use %s placeholders with a parameters tuple
options.why: Correct. Parameterized queries prevent SQL injection.
Constraint violations shouldn't be retried.

options.text: Raise statement_timeout to several hours for safety
options.why: Web apps typically use short timeouts (5–30 seconds).

questions.hint: Reuse connections, and never build SQL from strings.
questions.explain: Pool connections, parameterize queries, set sensible timeouts, and retry only transient errors.
